harnesses.notes: Mimir writes the file-based managed tier. An MDM profile for com.anthropic.claudecode ranks above the file and, with the default managedSourcesBehavior 'first-wins', hides Mimir's file completely. Deploy settings for Claude Code through Mimir only. Since v2.1.242, setting managedSourcesBehavior to 'merge' in the highest-ranked source (the MDM profile) makes Claude Code compose every admin source instead of hiding lower ones — an org that wants both an MDM profile and Mimir's file applied must opt in there, not in Mimir's file. Claude Code also reads a managed-settings.d/*.json drop-in directory alongside managed-settings.json, merged alphabetically (scalars last-wins, lists union+dedupe, nested blocks merge-by-field); Mimir does not write into that directory yet. New keys confirmed this review: allowedProviders, requiredMinimumVersion/requiredMaximumVersion, maxEffortLevel, disableAllHooks, allowedHttpHookUrls/httpHookAllowedEnvVars, sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly, sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly, strictPluginOnlyCustomization, and allowClaudeInChromeWithManagedMcp (a grant that loosens a default block — defaulted to anyFalse since unsure, so any source withholding it keeps the feature blocked).

outputs.description: Managed settings (highest file-based precedence; users cannot override).

harnesses.notes: Claude Desktop only reads the com.anthropic.claudefordesktop managed-preferences domain; there is no file-based alternative. Mimir writes that plist in /Library/Managed Preferences directly, which Apple does not document for third parties: macOS may remove it when profiles change, and Mimir restores it within seconds. Do not also deploy a vendor profile for this domain. Claude Desktop reads policy at launch; users must restart the app. CHANGED since last review: vendor docs describe managed preferences as read per-user (/Library/Managed Preferences/<user>/com.anthropic.claudefordesktop.plist), not the single device-wide file Mimir's compiled-in allowlist and this catalog's output path model — needs a Mimir change, see PR notes. Vendor docs also list many more managed keys than previously catalogued; this review only adds requireCoworkFullVmSandbox (cross-confirmed from the Claude Code docs too). The rest were seen in a lower-confidence source (summarized, not raw HTML) and are deliberately left out pending a direct-fetch confirmation pass.

outputs.description: Enterprise policy keys for Claude Desktop.

harnesses.notes: Mimir writes the system managed config, which overrides global, project and remote (.well-known/opencode) config. An MDM profile for ai.opencode.managed also overrides everything and conflicts with Mimir's output. Full precedence (lowest to highest), confirmed against the opencode source: remote (.well-known/opencode) < global < OPENCODE_CONFIG < project < .opencode/ dirs < OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT < Mimir's managed file dir < the ai.opencode.managed mobileconfig. opencode has no per-MCP-server allow/deny list; governance is only via remote-provided servers with a per-server enabled toggle. The 'strictest' ordering used below for share/permission.* is Mimir's own more-restrictive-wins policy choice, not a vendor-documented cross-source merge rule — opencode's own docs only describe plain tier override.

outputs.description: Managed opencode.json (keys: mcp, permission, provider, model, disabled_providers, enabled_providers, share, autoupdate, …).

harnesses.notes: requirements.toml holds hard constraints users cannot change (deployed locally or via an MDM profile for com.openai.codex using the requirements_toml_base64 key); managed_config.toml holds managed defaults the user can still override at runtime (MDM key config_toml_base64). Precedence is requirements.toml > cloud-managed configuration defaults (ChatGPT Business/Enterprise) > managed_config.toml. CORRECTED this review (confirmed against the codex-rs source): allowed_sandbox_modes is NOT deprecated, it is still a live, actively-tested requirements.toml field alongside allowed_permission_profiles, where any profile omitted from the list (including future built-ins) is denied. managed_config.toml itself is the one being phased out — Codex's own source calls it a 'best effort' legacy layer being replaced by requirements.toml, and it is already fully removed on Windows. Codex's own internal cross-source composition for the allowed_* fields is actually last-layer-wins override, not intersect; the 'intersect' strategy below is a deliberate Mimir-side policy choice (stricter than Codex's native default) layered on top of that, not a mirror of vendor behavior.

outputs.description: Legacy/deprecated managed defaults layered above the user's config.toml (approval_policy, sandbox_mode, otel telemetry block, check_for_update_on_startup, …); OpenAI is phasing this file out in favor of requirements.toml and has already removed it on Windows.

harnesses.notes: CONFIRMED device-level mechanism (re-verified this review against the raw docs in google-gemini/gemini-cli), genuine candidate for 'supported'. Casing confirmed exact: system overrides at /Library/Application Support/GeminiCli/settings.json, defaults at system-defaults.json in the same folder (env override: GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_SETTINGS_PATH). Precedence System overrides > Workspace > User > System defaults (arrays/objects merge rather than replace). Keys: tools.core (array, tool/command allowlist -> union), tools.sandbox (string enforce e.g. 'docker'), mcp.allowed (confirmed true allow-list, intersect: 'a server must be permitted by every source to run') + mcpServers (canonical server defs, union-by-name, System > Workspace > User on name collisions), telemetry.enabled / telemetry.logPrompts (bool kill switches -> anyFalse), privacy.usageStatisticsEnabled (bool -> anyFalse), security.disableYoloMode (bool lock -> anyTrue), security.auth.enforcedType (string, last/admin wins). excludeTools/tools.exclude is now deprecated in favor of policy-engine deny rules. The TOML policy engine ([[rule]] with toolName/decision/priority, plus richer fields subagent/mcpName/toolAnnotations/commandRegex/modes/denyMessage) loaded from Admin dirs (/Library/Application Support/GeminiCli/policies on macOS) uses a 5-tier priority system (Default=1, Extension=2, Workspace=3 [currently non-functional, see gemini-cli#18186], User=4, Admin=5); Admin always outranks the others. The admin policy directory is ignored entirely if it isn't root-owned and non-group/other-writable — Mimir must write it with those exact permissions. Recommend promoting to supported.

CHANGED since last review: a genuine on-device mechanism now exists (GA 2026-07-01, extended to CLI/VS Code 2026-07-08) making this a strong candidate for 'supported'. Two device-level channels, both read by Copilot CLI: (1) native MDM managed preferences for the com.github.copilot domain (macOS profile, string values only with dot-separated nested keys and JSON-encoded arrays/objects; Windows equivalent HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\GitHubCopilot); (2) file-based deployment at /Library/Application Support/GitHubCopilot/managed-settings.json on macOS (/etc/github-copilot/managed-settings.json on Linux, no native MDM on Linux) - file must be owned by root, not group/world-writable, no symlinks; client restart required to reload. Precedence: MDM-managed > server-managed (org's copilot/managed-settings.json in .github-private, legacy path .github/copilot/settings.json) > file-based > user's own ~/.copilot/config.json — EXCEPT sandbox and permissions.deny/ask/allow, which vendor docs say are composed in the most restrictive direction across delivery methods regardless of this precedence. Keys, re-confirmed directly from github/docs source this review: allowedMcpServers is vendor-documented, verbatim, as intersect ('a server must be permitted by every source to run'); permissions.allow is likewise documented as intersect, not union — same non-obvious stricter-than-expected pattern; deniedMcpServers and permissions.deny/ask are union, deny always wins; permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode is a string enum ('disable'/'unmanaged'), not a boolean, but still anyTrue-shaped (any source setting 'disable' wins); model (string, top-level key now supersedes legacy permissions.model, last/highest-precedence layer wins); enabledPlugins (union); extraKnownMarketplaces/strictKnownMarketplaces (most-restrictive wins). New keys found this review: autoTier (ordered tier, strictest wins), remoteControl, a richer telemetry object (enabled/endpoint/protocol/captureContent/lockCaptureContent/…), features.computerUse (anyFalse kill switch), and a {"overridable": value} wrapper on many keys enabling enterprise-vs-team-level overrides — a merge dimension not yet modeled here. Caveat still open as of 2026-10-01: GitHub issue github/copilot-cli#4959 shows the managed 'model' key is not reliably applied in non-interactive CLI runs (-p/piped stdin) as of CLI 1.0.89-1 - a known, unresolved bug, not a documentation gap; interactive sessions honor it. Recommend promoting to supported once that CLI bug is confirmed fixed, or shipping the file-based /Library/Application Support/GitHubCopilot/managed-settings.json output now with a note about the interactive-only model-key caveat.

CHANGED since last review: cursor.com/docs/enterprise/deployment-patterns now documents a genuine device-level mechanism — a macOS .mobileconfig configuration profile (a reference profile for the current bundle ID, com.todesktop.230313mzl4w4u92, ships inside Cursor.app's own Resources), deployable via Jamf/Kandji/Intune or by hand. Documented keys include AllowedExtensions, AllowedTeamId, WorkspaceTrustEnabled, UpdateMode, NetworkDisableHttp2 and ExtensionGalleryServiceUrl, each overriding user/workspace settings outright (no union semantics documented at this layer). CORRECTED this review: the MCP allow-list surface actually has two paths, not one — ~/.cursor/permissions.json (user) AND <workspace>/.cursor/permissions.json (per-repo) — and vendor docs describe them as concatenated/combined across scopes (mcpAllowlist -> union), not override; either can also be dropped in place by MDM at the device level. Candidate for 'supported' once the full key list and merge semantics inside the shipped .mobileconfig are read directly from a live environment (this run was again unable to get a direct page fetch of cursor.com, only corroborating search snippets).

Re-verified this review by fetching github.com/microsoft/vscode-docs' raw policies.md directly: VS Code's chat/MCP policy surface is much larger than previously catalogued (~28 chat/MCP-adjacent policies, not 8) and 'chat.mcp.access' is actually the VS Code *setting id* that the policy named ChatMCP maps to, not a policy name itself. Confirmed directly: policy values override the setting at every level (default/user/workspace), and ChatAgentDeniedNetworkDomains explicitly takes precedence over ChatAgentAllowedNetworkDomains (deny wins). Other policy-relevant keys worth modeling if promoted: ChatAllowedMcpServers/ChatDeniedMcpServers (deny wins), ChatAllowManagedMcpServersOnly (lock), ChatAgentSandboxEnabled/AllowNetwork/AllowUnsandboxedCommands, TelemetryLevel, EnableFeedback, ExtensionsAutoUpdateDelay, ChatApprovedAccountOrganizations, UpdateMode/ExtensionsAutoUpdate. VS Code Insiders reads a separate domain, com.microsoft.VSCodeInsiders (unconfirmed this review). Separately (and layered on top, per GitHub's 2026-07-08 changelog), GitHub's own com.github.copilot MDM domain / GitHubCopilot managed-settings.json — see the github-copilot-cli entry — now also applies to the Copilot Chat extension inside VS Code. Precedence between VS Code's native chat.* policy and GitHub's managed-settings layer is still not documented anywhere official; needs research before promoting to 'supported'.

CHANGED since last review: Cognition rebranded Windsurf to Devin Desktop on 2026-06-02 (same app, same com.exafunction.windsurf bundle ID kept for compatibility); canonical docs moved to docs.devin.ai/desktop/enterprise-policies, which docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/enterprise-policies still mirrors. That page confirms a device-level mechanism: a macOS .mobileconfig configuration profile, with a sample shipped inside the app bundle, deployable via MDM or by hand — separate from VS Code's own policy surface. Search snippets suggest keys for an MCP server allowlist, a managed-MCP-only lock, and telemetry/feedback toggles, but this run could not fetch the live page directly (egress-blocked) to confirm exact key names/types, so no mergeRules are added yet. Needs one direct read of docs.devin.ai/desktop/enterprise-policies before promoting to 'supported'.

Only user-level YAML config (~/.config/goose/config.yaml), plus sibling permission.yaml/secrets.yaml. Needs a YAML writer and a per-user output mode. New this review (confirmed against the official repo's docs source): an admin MCP/extension allowlist exists via the GOOSE_ALLOWLIST env var, pointed at a YAML file (hosted anywhere, edit-access-restricted) listing permitted extensions ({id, command}); if unset, no restriction applies. It is a restriction allowlist (intersect-shaped) but is delivered via an externally-hosted file referenced by an env var, not a local device file Mimir can write directly — still not a 'supported' candidate, but no longer 'no admin mechanism at all'.
Enterprise policy (allowedMCPServers, yoloModeAllowed) is delivered via Cline's remote config, not a device file. Runs as a VS Code extension.

Could not find a credible, maintained official project under this exact name this review. The most-referenced same-named repos appear to be repo-squatting/SEO-spam or parody projects (one self-describes as 'an agent-managed museum exhibit' with implausible star counts, explicitly disclaims affiliation, and tells users it has been renamed to a different project, 'agent-code'). No official vendor site, docs, or maintained GitHub org could be confirmed. Leaving this entry as-is (no outputs, no documentation link) rather than encode any detail from a low-trust source; a future review should check whether 'agent-code' or another canonical name is the real successor.

CORRECTED this review: Kiro CLI is AWS's rebrand of Amazon Q Developer CLI; secondary sources place the rebrand at 2025-11-17, not 2026-11-17 as previously (and implausibly, given a 2026-10-05 review date) recorded — kiro.dev itself was egress-blocked this run, so the exact date is still not primary-sourced. Also corrected: the managed preference domain referenced in the update-management doc is dev.kiro.desktop, not dev.kiro.cli, and it is scoped only to the desktop IDE's auto-updater (keys UpdateUrl, UpdateMode — UpdateMode='none' always disables updates regardless of UpdateUrl). Per-user CLI settings live at ~/.kiro/settings/cli.json (plain JSON). Fleet-wide 'permission policies' described under kiro.dev/docs/enterprise/governance/permissions/ read as a cloud/admin-console mechanism, not a local macOS file. No confirmed device-level managed-settings file/domain for general CLI policy — needs more research before adding outputs.

Terminal coding agent from Factory AI; installed via install script, Homebrew cask (droid) or npm. Settings at ~/.factory/settings.json with a ~/.factory/settings.local.json override and a project-level .factory/settings.local.json. New this review: an 'Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings' doc describes a 4-level settings hierarchy (Org > Folder > Project > User), each level a .factory/ folder with its own settings.json, covering model policy, network restrictions and autonomy ceilings — org level is admin-owned and highest-priority among them. This reads as org/cloud-distributed configuration (a central bundle or config endpoint), not a macOS-device/MDM-dropped file — still not a 'supported' candidate, but no longer 'no admin mechanism found'. Exact key names and precedence vs. CLI flags are unconfirmed (docs.factory.ai access was blocked this run; based on search snippets) — needs a direct fetch before adding outputs.

CHANGED since last review: Terminal coding agent from Sourcegraph; npm package @ampcode/cli (formerly @sourcegraph/amp, still supported), now a single-file Bun-compiled executable. Global config at ~/.config/amp/settings.json/.jsonc; workspace .amp/settings.json overrides it (searched upward to repo root), except keymaps. A genuine OS-level managed-settings file is now documented: macOS /Library/Application Support/ampcode/managed-settings.json (Linux /etc/ampcode/managed-settings.json, Windows C:\ProgramData\ampcode\managed-settings.json), with keys amp.mcpServers, amp.mcpPermissions (allow/block MCP servers) and amp.permissions (allow/block bash command patterns), plus the ability to override any other setting. This directly supersedes the prior 'not a device-level file' conclusion and is a genuine 'supported' candidate — but /Library/Application Support/ampcode/ is not yet in Mimir's compiled-in path allowlist, so no output is added here (see PR notes, Needs Mimir change). ampcode.com was egress-blocked for a direct fetch this run (based on search snippets of the two new URLs above); precedence of managed-settings.json vs. user/workspace settings and the exact allow/deny semantics of amp.mcpServers should be re-confirmed with a direct fetch before adding mergeRules.

New entry. Native macOS terminal with a built-in Agent Mode. User settings live in ~/.warp/settings.toml (TOML, not JSON). Enterprise policy (agent autonomy, model allowlists, secret redaction, sharing) is enforced through a cloud-based Admin Panel for teams, not a macOS device-level MDM profile or managed-preferences domain — not a managed-config candidate until an on-device mechanism is documented. App bundle ID not confirmed from an official source this run, so omitted from detect.

New entry. Meta's coding agent CLI (beta 2026-08-05, GA 2026-08-31), running on the Muse Spark model; installed via a curl install script producing a `muse` binary. Docs reference `muse config validate --plane <defaults|policy>` and a `managed_hooks_path`, suggesting an admin policy mechanism exists, but this run could not confirm an exact macOS managed-config file path/domain from an official source — needs research before adding outputs.

Open-source terminal coding agent (TUI) from Charm; installed via Homebrew (charmbracelet/tap/crush) or npm (@charmland/crush). CORRECTED this review (confirmed via a direct fetch of the repo README): crush.json is now explicitly called legacy/deprecated; the primary config is crushrc, a Bash script with Crush-specific builtins (provider add, model add, permissions allow, mcp add), loaded in priority ./.crushrc > ./crushrc > ~/.config/crush/crushrc. crush.json (schema at charm.land/crush.json) still works but is secondary. Both crushrc and crush.json run as trusted code at load time (crushrc is full shell; $(...) in crush.json executes) — relevant to how much Mimir should trust a project-local config file. No enterprise/MDM mechanism documented — individual-developer tool as of this review.

New entry. Open-source terminal coding agent CLI from the Qwen team, forked from Gemini CLI and optimized for Qwen3-Coder models; codebase search/edit, shell execution and MCP support. Installed via npm (@qwen-code/qwen-code) or Homebrew (qwen-code). No enterprise/admin/managed-config mechanism found in the repo README — needs research, though as a Gemini CLI fork it may eventually inherit a similar mechanism.

New entry. Open-source git-native terminal AI pair-programming CLI that edits repos via model-generated diffs, using tree-sitter/PageRank codebase mapping. Installed via `python -m pip install aider-install && aider-install` (pipx also common). Config file .aider.conf.yml, loaded in priority from the user's home directory, the git repo root, then the current working directory. No enterprise/admin/MDM mechanism found in the fetched docs/README.

New entry. Agentic coding CLI from Augment Code, built on Augment's 'context engine'; analyzes/edits codebases from natural language and integrates with GitHub Actions CI. Installed via npm (@augmentcode/auggie, requires Node.js 22+). Project-level custom commands in .augment/commands/*.md; user-level settings under ~/.augment. No enterprise/admin/MDM mechanism found in the fetched docs — oriented at individual developers and CI.

New entry. Self-hosted 'developer control center' for running coding agents (its own OpenHands agent, or others such as Claude Code/Codex) locally, remotely or in the cloud; formerly known as OpenDevin. Installed via npm (@openhands/agent-canvas) or a Docker image. Offers 'OpenHands Cloud' and 'OpenHands Enterprise' as paid hosted/multi-agent-server products with a self-hosting security-hardening guide, but no macOS device-level/MDM managed-config mechanism was found.
